lead: This unit makes the browser programmable. You start with plain JavaScript, learn to change the page through events and the DOM, handle work that finishes later, and talk to a server without reloading the page. After it you can build a small interactive front end, read and write XML and JSON, and follow the jQuery in older code.
about: Unit 3 turns a static HTML page into a running program. Chapter 3.1 starts with JavaScript values, operators and control statements; 3.2 packs those steps into functions and stores many values in arrays and objects. 3.3 and 3.4 connect code to the page: events fire handlers, and the DOM tree is read and rewritten to give dynamic HTML. 3.5 adds the ES6 syntax — let, const, arrow functions, classes, modules — that modern code and React assume. 3.6 explains why JavaScript must be asynchronous; 3.7 uses that machinery to fetch data from a server with XMLHttpRequest and JSON. 3.8 steps back to XML, DTD and XML Schema, the data formats AJAX grew around. 3.9 closes with jQuery, the shorthand library still found in legacy code.

chapters.idea: A JavaScript program is a list of statements: variables hold values, operators combine them, and control statements decide which lines run.
chapters.depth: How a script sits in a page (inline <script>, external file, defer) and where output appears (console.log, alert). Data types: number, string, boolean, null, undefined, object, symbol, bigint; typeof; automatic type coercion. Declarations with var, let and const, and the difference in scope and re-declaration. Operators: arithmetic (+ - * / % **), assignment, comparison (==, ===, !=, !==), logical (&&, ||, !), ternary ?: and nullish ??. Control: if, if-else, else-if ladder, switch with break and default, for, while, do-while, for-of, break and continue. Some syllabi write the exam question as a program that demonstrates variables and operators, so keep two small full programs ready.

figure.title: Grade ladder for marks = 72
figure.caption: 72 fails 90 and fails 75, so it stops at the third test and prints C.
figure.aria: A decision ladder: marks 72 tested against 90, then 75, then 60, with each test branching to a print step.

chapters.example: A student scores 72 out of 100. Write an else-if ladder, and an equivalent switch, that prints A for 90 or above, B for 75 or above, C for 60 or above, and D otherwise. Then write a for loop that prints the sum 1+2+3+4+5. State every output.
chapters.trap: Using == where === is meant: '5' == 5 is true but '5' === 5 is false. Second trap: a var declared inside a block leaks out, and a switch case with no break falls through into the next case.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 (an HTML page to hold the script), Unit 1 (the browser console).
chapters.leave: Arrow functions and classes to 3.5, page changes to 3.4, timers and delayed work to 3.6.

chapters.idea: A function names a block of steps you can call again, an array stores many values in order, and an object stores many values under names.
chapters.depth: Function declaration against function expression; parameters and arguments; return, and the undefined result when nothing is returned; default parameters; rest (...args). Scope and hoisting in one short block. Recursion with one small example (factorial or sum of digits). Arrays: literal, length, index, push/pop, shift/unshift, splice/slice, concat, join, indexOf/includes, sort with a comparator, and the callback methods map, filter, reduce, forEach. Objects: literal syntax, dot and bracket access, methods, nested objects, Object.keys/values/entries, deleting a property. The Date object and Math.round/toFixed when money or marks are printed. One line each for built-ins — this is not a reference manual.

figure.title: map adds 5 grace marks
figure.caption: map builds a new row; the original marks row is left as it was.
figure.aria: Two rows of four cells: marks 45, 72, 90, 38 and the same marks after adding five, giving 50, 77, 95, 43.

chapters.example: marks = [45, 72, 90, 38]. (a) Write a function average(a) that adds the values with a loop and returns the mean. (b) Use filter to keep marks of 60 or more. (c) Use map to add 5 grace marks to every mark. Give all three results.
chapters.trap: Thinking map and filter change the original array. sort() without a comparator compares as strings, so [10, 9, 1] becomes [1, 10, 9]. A function that forgets return gives undefined, not the last value.
chapters.leave: Arrow function syntax and classes to 3.5, JSON text conversion to 3.7, this inside callbacks to 3.5.

chapters.idea: An event is a signal from the browser that something happened, and a handler is the function you register to run when it fires.
chapters.depth: Terms: event, event source, listener, handler, event object. Three ways to attach — inline attribute, element property (onclick), addEventListener — and removeEventListener. The event object: type, target, currentTarget, key, clientX. preventDefault and stopPropagation. The three phases: capture down, target, bubble up; event delegation with one listener on a parent list. Events worth knowing: click, dblclick, change, input, submit, keydown, mouseover, load, DOMContentLoaded, resize, scroll. Child-to-parent communication in components is a React idea and belongs to Unit 5.

figure.title: Capture down, bubble up
figure.caption: The click travels down to the button, then back up; the div's normal listener runs on the way back.
figure.aria: A click moves from window capture to div capture to the button target, then back up through the div and window in the bubble phase.

chapters.example:
A page contains
. A click listener on the button logs 'button'; one on the div logs 'div'. (a) Clicking the button logs in which order? (b) What changes if the button handler calls event.stopPropagation()? (c) What if the div listener was added with {capture:true}?
chapters.trap: Forgetting preventDefault on a form submit, so the page reloads and wipes all your output. Also expecting the outer handler to run first when it is an ordinary bubble listener.
chapters.leave: The full element tree and selection to 3.4, jQuery event shorthand to 3.9, React event props to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: The browser parses HTML into a tree of nodes called the DOM, and changing that tree from JavaScript is what dynamic HTML means.
chapters.depth: The DOM as a tree: document → html → head/body; node types element, text, attribute; parent, child, sibling. Selecting: getElementById, getElementsByClassName, getElementsByTagName, querySelector, querySelectorAll, and why a NodeList is not an array. Reading and writing: textContent against innerHTML, value on inputs, getAttribute/setAttribute, classList with add/remove/toggle/contains, style properties. Building: createElement, createTextNode, appendChild, insertBefore, remove, replaceChildren. BOM: window, location (href for a page redirect), history, navigator, screen, alert/confirm/prompt, setTimeout and setInterval as BOM calls. Cookies and sessions are server-side and sit in Unit 4.

figure.caption: The script walks this tree: it renames the h1, adds a second li under ul#items and marks the first li.
figure.aria: Tree of the example page: document holds html, which holds head with the title and body with a heading and a list containing one item.

chapters.example:
Page:

Cart

  • Pen
. Write a script that (a) sets the heading text to 'Cart: 2 items', (b) appends a new li with text 'Tea', (c) gives the first li the class 'red', and (d) reports document.querySelectorAll('#items li').length before and after step (b).
chapters.trap: innerHTML with user text opens an XSS hole and destroys listeners inside the element, so prefer textContent. Also querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList while getElementsByClassName returns a live collection that changes as the page changes.
chapters.leave: XSS and server-side validation to Unit 6, virtual DOM rendering to Unit 5, jQuery selectors to 3.9.

chapters.idea: ES6 (also called ES2015) added block-scoped let and const, arrow functions, classes and modules, so large JavaScript can be split into readable pieces.
chapters.depth: let and const against var: block scope, temporal dead zone, no re-declaration, const binds the name and not the object. Template literals with backticks and ${}. Destructuring of arrays and objects; spread and rest. Arrow functions: shorter form, no own this or arguments, and when not to use one as an object method. Classes: constructor, methods, extends, super, static, a getter in one line. Modules: named and default export, the matching import forms, one module per file, and why the browser needs type='module'. Also for-of, Map and Set, and enhanced object literals. Promises are named here only; they are taught in 3.6.

figure.caption: A let or const name lives only inside its block; a var name is visible in the whole function.
figure.aria: Nested scopes: a block inside a function inside the global scope, with var names in the outer regions and let and const names inside the block.

chapters.example: for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); } prints what? Rewrite the loop with let and give the new output. Then rewrite function add(a, b) { return a + b; } as an arrow function and evaluate add(2, 3).
chapters.trap: Assuming const freezes an object: const o = {}; o.x = 1 works fine. And an arrow function used as a method has no own this, so it does not see the object.
chapters.prereq: 3.1, 3.2 and 3.4 (code that will be rewritten in ES6).
chapters.leave: Promise behaviour to 3.6, JSX and React components to Unit 5, TypeScript types to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: JavaScript runs one task at a time on a single call stack, so slow work is handed to the browser and its result is picked up later by the event loop.
chapters.depth: Call stack, Web APIs, task queue (macrotasks) and microtask queue. The rule: the stack must be empty, and all microtasks drain, before the next timer callback. Callbacks and callback hell; promises with states pending/fulfilled/rejected, then/catch/finally, chaining, Promise.all, Promise.race, Promise.allSettled. async/await with try/catch, and running requests in parallel with Promise.all instead of awaiting inside a loop. Timers: setTimeout, setInterval, clearTimeout, clearInterval, and the number of milliseconds.

figure.title: Order of output for A, B, C, D
figure.caption: The promise callback C jumps ahead of timer B even though the timer was set first.
figure.aria: Synchronous logs A and D finish first; the promise callback is queued as a microtask and runs before the timer callback B.

chapters.example: Predict the output order: console.log('A'); setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C')); console.log('D'); Then explain why C comes before B.
chapters.trap: Thinking setTimeout(fn, 0) runs immediately, and reading an async function's result without await — you get a pending promise, not the value.
chapters.leave: The Node.js event loop and its phases to Unit 6, Promise-based fetch calls to 3.7, RxJS observables to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: AJAX means asking the server for data in the background and patching the page with the reply, without a full page reload.
chapters.depth: What AJAX stands for, and the client-server path: browser → XMLHttpRequest → web server → response → DOM update. The XMLHttpRequest object: new XMLHttpRequest(), open(method, url, async), setRequestHeader, send(body), readyState 0 to 4, status 200/404/500, responseText against responseXML, onreadystatechange and the newer onload/onerror — the call-back method some syllabi name. GET against POST with a form-encoded body. JSON: syntax rules (double quotes, no trailing comma, no functions), JSON.parse, JSON.stringify, JSON against XML in a short table. fetch() as the modern promise-based call, one example. CORS in one line. The server that answers these calls is built in Unit 6.

figure.caption: The page never reloads; only the #out element is rewritten.
figure.aria: The page asks the XHR object to send a GET; the server answers 200 with a JSON body; the XHR reports readyState 4 and the page writes the result into the DOM.

chapters.example: A server returns [{"name":"Asha","marks":72}] at /api/marks.json. Write the XMLHttpRequest code that fetches it and writes 'Asha: 72' into <div id='out'>. List the readyState values you pass through, and say what your code does if the server answers 404.
chapters.trap: Updating the page on readyState 4 alone without checking status 200, so an error page's HTML lands in your div. Also calling JSON.parse on a response that fetch() already parsed.
chapters.prereq: 3.4 (writing into the page) and 3.6 (callbacks or promises).
chapters.leave: Building the REST endpoint to Unit 6, XML parsing detail to 3.8, $.ajax to 3.9.

chapters.idea: XML writes data as a tree of tags, and a DTD or an XML Schema is a contract saying which tags and attributes may appear and in what order.
chapters.depth: XML declaration, elements, attributes, nesting, the single root, case sensitivity, comments, CDATA, entities, namespaces (xmlns) in one line. Well-formed against valid; XML against HTML. DTD: <!DOCTYPE>, <!ELEMENT> with (#PCDATA), EMPTY, ANY, child sequences and the occurrence symbols ? * +, <!ATTLIST> with #REQUIRED, #IMPLIED and defaults. XML Schema: xs:schema, xs:element with name and type, xs:complexType with xs:sequence, xs:simpleType with xs:restriction, built-in types xs:string, xs:integer, xs:decimal, xs:date, and minOccurs/maxOccurs. Why XSD can type-check and a DTD cannot. A DTD against XSD comparison table. Parsing with DOMParser and responseXML mentioned only.

figure.caption: The DTD or schema allows exactly this shape: one bookstore, one or more books, title before price.
figure.aria: The example XML as a tree: bookstore contains a book with id b1, and the book contains title Web Tech and price 350.

chapters.example: Write XML for one book: title 'Web Tech', price 350, attribute id='b1'. Then write a DTD that allows one or more books, each with a required title followed by a price, and an XSD fragment that forces price to be xs:integer. Finally: is <price>₹350</price> valid?
chapters.trap: Treating well-formed and valid as the same thing, forgetting the single root element, and expecting a DTD to reject a non-numeric price — a DTD treats every value as text, only XSD can type-check.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 (tag and attribute syntax) and 3.7 (XML as an AJAX reply).
chapters.leave: XSLT and server-side XML to later reading, JSON against XML comparison kept short in 3.7.

chapters.idea: jQuery is a small library that wraps selection, events and AJAX in short chained calls that behave the same in every browser.
chapters.depth: Adding jQuery from a CDN or a local file, and one line on why it mattered when browsers disagreed. The $ function and jQuery objects that wrap a set of elements; $(document).ready and the shorthand $(function(){}). CSS selectors plus filters such as :first, :even, :input. Getters and setters: text, html, val, attr, css, addClass/removeClass/toggleClass, data. Adding and removing: append, prepend, before, after, remove, empty. Effects: hide, show, fadeIn, fadeOut, slideUp with a duration in milliseconds. Events: click, on, off, and each for looping. AJAX: $.ajax with url, method and dataType 'json', plus $.get, $.post and their done/fail callbacks. Chaining returns the same jQuery object; .get(0) or [0] gives the real DOM element.

figure.title: One selection, three chained calls
figure.caption: Each call returns the same set of elements, which is why the dots fit on one line.
figure.aria: One selection of list items flows through a colour change, a class add and a fade in; each call returns the same set.

chapters.example:
A page has
  • Pen
  • Book
  • Bag
. Write one jQuery chain that adds the class 'sel' to all three items and sets the first item's text to 'Pen (new)'. Then use .each() to print every item's text. Give the console output.
chapters.trap: Expecting $('#items li').text() to return all the texts — on a set it returns only the first element's text. And confusing the jQuery object with the DOM element; use [0] or .get(0).
chapters.leave: Modern fetch and framework data calls to Unit 5 and Unit 6, effects animation detail to the jQuery reference.
